draft. A subsequent user or assistant entry consumes the draft. `history_tree()`
provides a pure, depth-annotated view of all visible branches.

`copy_branch()` copies one connected path, including an inactive path selected
for fork, under the source run lock. It remaps IDs and context cuts, preserves
timestamps, and omits navigation/checkpoint/recovery controls and siblings. The copy
is written as one snapshot, or remains deferred when it has no conversation.

Log-only checkpoint and restore events coordinate recovery. Checkpoints link an earlier
user entry and pre-turn ancestor. Restore parents identify the committed target;
code-only restore must preserve the preceding head. File effects and LIFO state
belong to the workspace coordinator, not conversation projection.

## Listing and titles

`list_sessions(directory)` returns session ID, update time, and a title derived
from the first user text across the full file, even when navigation currently
precedes that input. Corrupt files are skipped so one bad session cannot
break the list. Update time and ordering use file modification time, so copied
historical timestamps do not make a newly created session appear old.

## Invariants

- Entries are never rewritten in place.
- IDs are unique within a file.
- A parent precedes its child.
- The file ends with exactly one newline.
- The schema is closed; new event types require a decision record.

## Tests

`test_log.py` covers create, append, resume, tail repair, cache isolation,
external changes, failed sync, and listing.
`test_session_history.py` covers navigation, old-format recovery, inactive
forks, and independent copies. `test_projection.py` covers malformed paths.
`test_history_e2e.py` verifies the public commands through real TUI input.

# Projection and request

<!-- source: subsystems/projection-request.md -->

# Projection and request

## Projection

`project(entries)` is pure. It:

1. Finds the latest `system` entry.
2. Applies the latest `window` start.
3. Applies the latest `compaction` cut and emits a summary message.
4. Converts user, assistant, and tool-result facts to messages.
5. Pairs each tool call with its result by call ID.
6. Inserts a synthetic interrupted result if the branch ends inside a call.

It rejects orphan results, duplicate results, and cuts that do not point to a
user entry. The projection does not call a provider or write the log.

## Request

`build(conversation, tools, budget, context)`:

1. Joins the base system prompt with request-only context.
2. Estimates tokens.
3. Preserves all projected messages and tool bodies.
4. Converts to provider messages and tool definitions.
5. Returns a `Request` and a `BuildReport`.

`BuildReport` records estimated tokens and budget. Legacy dropped-call and
turn counters remain empty/zero. `require_sendable()` raises `RequestTooLarge`
when the full request cannot fit. The loop reduces context only through logged
compaction and window decisions, then rejects any remaining overflow.

## Context order

The system message carries base instructions plus, in order: instructions,
skill catalog, NOTE, memory, and goal. These inputs are request-only; the
The request audit records their full text, the admitted messages, tool definitions,
non-authentication options, and budget. Session files can contain sensitive input.

## Tests

`test_projection.py`, `test_request.py`, and
`test_compaction.py` cover cuts, strict admission, and wire-format contracts.

# Loop

<!-- source: subsystems/loop.md -->

# Loop

`run(log, text, ...)` is the only stage that writes during a turn.

## One run

1. Append the `user` fact.
2. For each step:
   - Project the branch.
   - If the full estimate exceeds budget, call the compactor.
   - Build the request.
   - If still over, call the window fallback.
   - Append a `request` audit fact.
   - Stream the provider.
   - Append the assistant fact.
   - Resolve and execute each tool call.
   - Append tool-result facts.
3. Append one `run` fact with termination, steps, usage, and error.

## Provider handling

The loop collects text deltas, tool calls, usage, and provider replay state. A
failure becomes an `attempt` fact. Retryable failures are retried once by
default; the retry delay is configurable. A terminal failure ends the run with
`provider_error` and never creates an assistant fact.

## Termination

- `completed`: the provider ended without tool calls.
- `step_limit`: the configured step count was reached.
- `context_error`: no request fits after compaction and window fallback.
- `aborted`: cancellation was requested.
- `provider_error`: the provider failed.

## Cancellation

A cancellation token is checked between steps and tool calls. Running tools get
the token; remaining calls receive interrupted results. The run records the
reason in its `run` fact.

## Events

The host receives text deltas, tool start, tool end, and final output. Events are
presentation; facts are durable. A host can drop events without losing history.

## Tests

`test_loop.py` covers completion, tool use, approvals, retries, timeouts,
cancellation, context errors, and window fallback.

# Tools and policy

<!-- source: subsystems/tools-policy.md -->

# Tools and policy

## Contracts

A tool declares a name, description, JSON schema, and async `execute`. The loop
records content and the error flag; tools do not append session facts.

`harness.permissions.Policy.check` returns a `PermissionCheck` with a decision
(`allow`, `deny`, or `ask`), reason, and `ExecutionScope`. `authorize` resolves
only asks using an `ApprovalRequest` and `ApprovalResult`.
The loop and direct application calls use `harness.executor.execute_tool`.

`WorkspacePolicy` applies mode constraints and protected paths before explicit
rules, grants, and mode defaults. Matching rules use deny > ask > allow.
Subagent modes cannot expand parent permissions. See
[Tools and security](../tools-security.md) for user-facing semantics.

## Execution

The shared executor installs the authorized scope in a context variable only while the
specific tool runs. This scope is preserved across async tasks and worker
threads and reset afterward. It never changes the default workspace or grants.

Application assembly constructs a `PlatformSandbox` with the project root, private temp,
network setting, and protected paths. `SubprocessShell` wraps commands before
spawning. File tools use the same backend through `coding.tools._worker`; snapshot
storage remains host-owned. External file changes have no workspace snapshot.
Cancellation signals reach the subprocess launcher, and tools wait for process
termination before returning or cleaning up request files.

Linux uses bubblewrap, macOS uses Seatbelt, and Windows runs directly. Backend
errors become tool errors, not unsandboxed retries. MCP server processes are
trusted host extensions outside this boundary.

## Reviewer

`AutoReviewer` receives the authorization reason, exact arguments, retained
conversation, ancestor conversations, and context constraints. It uses a
separate tool-free request. Oversized input is rejected rather than silently
truncated. Output is a strict object with `allowed: bool` and `reason: str`.
Rejections and failures return their reasons to the model as tool errors.

## Tests

- `test_policy.py`: mode constraints, precedence, and write scope.
- `test_grants.py`: exact grants and scope isolation.
- `test_review.py`: strict responses and model-visible denial reasons.
- `test_subagents.py`: child permission ceilings.
- `test_sandbox.py`: real OS file/network isolation, worker integration,
  cancellation, Windows bypass, and unavailable backends.

# Context and compaction

<!-- source: subsystems/context-compaction.md -->

# Context and compaction

## Request context

The system message is the base prompt plus request-only context:

1. Project instructions from `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, or variants.
2. Skill catalog names and descriptions.
3. `NOTE.md` working state.
4. `MEMORY.md` durable facts.
5. An active goal.

The request audit records this context and the normalized request; it does not
turn the text into conversation facts.

`/context` summarizes the current request snapshot by its actual sources:
system prompt, project instructions, working note, memory, goal, skill catalog,
loaded skills, built-in tool schemas, MCP schemas, conversation, tool results,
and retained summaries. Optional categories appear when present. Delegation
tool schemas count as built-in tools; child conversations are not parent context.
Each token belongs to one category. Input remaining excludes the output reserve
and headroom.

File sources include loaded `AGENTS.md` or its fallback, notes, memory, skill
bodies and references, read files, and attachments. MCP sources list current
schema counts and token estimates per server, plus resources, prompts, and tool
results still present in the active conversation. A schema refresh changes the
schema list; loaded content remains until projection removes it.

For OpenAI Responses, `/context` calls the
[input token count endpoint](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/token-counting)
with the same converted input, instructions, tools, and response format used by
inference. The returned total is displayed as **Input (provider count)**. This
does not generate a reply or add a conversation event. Endpoint or account
errors are shown alongside the explicitly labeled fallback estimate.

For `deepseek-flash` and `deepseek-v4-pro`, the command uses the
[official V4 tokenizer](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/token_usage/)
through `tokenizers`. On first use, it downloads the public model archive and
caches the checksum-verified JSON under `~/.cade/tokenizers/`. Later inspections
work from that cache. Text uses model tokenization; message framing, images,
and server-side tool formatting still require an estimate. The report names
the tokenizer and does not label this total as a provider measurement.

Source breakdowns are estimates, not provider-supplied per-file billing data.
They use the selected model tokenizer when available, otherwise the character
heuristic. Input remaining uses the provider total when available. The latest
request's reported input/output usage remains separate from both current input
and cumulative run totals. Inspection does not contact MCP servers or modify
the conversation. Request admission retains its existing offline estimate;
normal model calls do not issue an additional pre-count request.

## Compaction

`Compactor` runs when the full projection exceeds the input budget.

1. Select the cut at a user boundary that keeps the recent tail under the
   configured target.
2. Serialize older messages, including a prior summary.
3. Ask the provider for a summary with a bounded output.
4. Append a `compaction` fact with summary and `first_kept_id`.
5. Reproject.

A summary failure or a cut with no messages appends an `attempt` fact and leaves
the conversation unchanged. A prior summary is included as `PRIOR SUMMARY`, so
compaction is iterative.

## Window fallback

If compaction cannot fit, the loop may call the window hook. The CLI starts a
window at the latest user entry with a fixed handoff that points to `NOTE.md`
and history. If the request still does not fit, the run terminates with
`context_error`.

## History

The `history` tool searches the branch or reads an exact entry or tool result.
It retrieves evidence outside the current compaction or window boundary.
Exact content is capped; search results point to entry IDs.

## Request admission

Admission preserves the full projection. Overflow requires a logged context
transition or fails with `context_error`. See
[Projection and request](projection-request.md).

## Tests

`test_compaction.py`, `test_window.py`, `test_history.py`, and
the request tests cover cuts, summaries, fallback, and retrieval.

# Extensions

<!-- source: subsystems/extensions.md -->

# Extensions

Extensions add behavior through narrow seams. None changes the session schema.

## Skills

Discovery reads skill metadata from user and trusted project roots. The request
carries a catalog; the `skill` tool loads a body or reference on demand and
returns resource paths. Activated instructions missing after compaction or a
window reset are restored from the active branch into request context. See
[Skills and memory](../skills-memory.md) for configuration and activation.

## Memory

`MEMORY.md` is request context. The `memory` tool appends one bullet and cannot
write other paths. The file is capped to protect the request budget.

## MCP

Each configured stdio or HTTP server keeps one connection. Discovery reads
`tools/list`; calls use `tools/call` over a serialized queue. Tools are prefixed
`mcp__`, ask by default, and are denied in plan and read-only modes. A server
that cannot start is reported and skipped.

## Subagents

`SubagentRunner` creates a child session under `<sessions>/subagents`. The child
gets the parent provider, budget, policy, approver, context, and base tools plus
its own history. It cannot spawn another subagent and is limited to
20 steps. The parent records only the call and summary. `DelegateTool` runs one
or more child tasks sequentially and optionally applies a more restrictive
child mode. Reviewer requests retain ancestor conversations so a child prompt
cannot replace human restrictions.

## Snapshots

`SnapshotStore` captures `write`, `edit`, and common single-command shell
mutations. `WorkspaceRecovery` coordinates checkpoint actions for CLI `--undo`
and TUI `/undo` and `/redo`. Snapshots are project state, not session facts.

## Goals

`GoalStore` persists one objective in `.cade/goal.json`. The `goal` tool and
`/goal` command manage it. An active goal is request context.

## Hosts

The terminal host runs one-shot tasks and the TUI. It uses the same loop and
policy as every other entry path.

## Limits

MCP capability and protocol boundaries are documented in
[MCP](../mcp.md). See [Subagents](../subagents.md) for child-session permissions
and sequential execution.

## Tests

`test_skills.py`, `test_memory.py`, `test_mcp.py`, `test_mcp_integration.py`, `test_subagents.py`,
`test_snapshots.py`, and `test_goal.py`.

# Tools and security

<!-- source: tools-security.md -->

# Tools and security

## Workspace tools

- `read`: read file text or attach an image. Output is capped at 2,000 lines or 50 KB.
- `write`: write UTF-8 text and create parent directories.
- `edit`: apply unique, non-overlapping replacements against the original file.
- `bash`, `powershell`: run a shell command, optionally with a workdir and
  `additional_write_paths` that request extra permissions for this call.
- `question`: collect choices or custom answers; dismissal stops the turn.
- `websearch`, `webfetch`: search or retrieve web content. With `network=false`,
  both are hidden from tool catalogs and model requests, including subagents.
  The execution policy still rejects stale calls on every platform.

Use `bash` or `powershell` for directory listings, file discovery, and content
search. These commands follow the shell's permissions and sandbox policy.
See the [tool catalog](design/tool-catalog.md) for parameters and limits.

The workspace is the fixed project root, not the shell's current directory or
an alias for the entire home directory. Reads can use external paths, except
protected files. Workspace writes have snapshots; external writes do not.

## Modes

- `build` is the default. Normal edits, tests, builds, and shell pipelines run
  automatically. Detected destructive, privileged, publishing, or external-send
  operations require approval.
- `ask` allows classified read-only operations and asks before changes or
  unclassified shell commands.
- `plan` supports exploration and discussion, not implementation. Project
  changes, memory changes, goal changes, and MCP calls are denied. File tools
  can write under `<workspace>/.cade-plans/` only after approval for a
  user-requested plan. Implementation requires the user to switch modes.

Subagents inherit the parent's limits. A child mode can only narrow them.
`--read-only` and `--sandbox read-only` deny mutations while allowing classified
read-only shell commands. These constraints cannot be overridden by rules,
grants, `--yes`, or Reviewer approval.

## Rules and grants

Rules in `cade.json` match a tool, normalized path subtree, or command
prefix. All matching rules participate: `deny` wins over `ask`, which wins over
`allow`. An explicit allow overrides a default ask, not an effective deny.
Remove or change a deny rule to revoke it; an approval answer cannot do that.

A TTY answer of `a` creates a process-local session grant. File grants match the
same tool and path. Shell grants also match workdir and extra write paths;
MCP grants match the complete arguments. A grant can answer an ask but cannot
bypass a deny. `/permissions` lists grants; `/permissions clear` removes them.

Explicit reads and writes of `.env*` files (except `.env.example`) and common
home credential paths such as `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, and `~/.config/gh` require
approval on every use. Detected shell access follows the same rule, including
relative paths resolved from `workdir`. Sensitive approvals do not create or
reuse session grants, and explicit deny rules still apply. Read-only external
Git commands remain allowed; detected mutations of external repositories
require approval. Approval does not expand the OS sandbox's write scope.

## Approvals and Reviewer

Only an `ask` enters approval:

- `--yes` approves asks, not denials.
- `--auto-review` sends the pending action, authorization reason, retained
  conversation, parent conversations, and context constraints to a tool-free
  Reviewer call. The response must contain a strict boolean `allowed` and a
  non-empty `reason`.
- Otherwise, a TTY prompts for `y` once, `n` deny, or `a` always.
- Without an available approver, the action is denied.

Reviewer rejection, timeout, provider failure, and malformed responses become
error tool results with reasons. They return to the acting model without an
automatic human prompt. The model must respect the denial while adjusting its
approach. Reviewer does not inspect every ordinary development operation.

Shell classification and risk detection are conservative heuristics, not a
security boundary or a complete analysis of arbitrary scripts. They cannot
identify every destructive or external effect hidden inside programs.

## OS sandbox

Filesystem scope is independent of mode and approval:

| Policy | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| `workspace-write` (default) | Write in the project and private session temp directory |
| `read-only` | No regular file writes |
| `danger-full-access` | Skip OS confinement; explicit deny rules still apply |

Linux uses installed `bwrap` (bubblewrap). macOS uses system `sandbox-exec`
(Seatbelt). Missing backends and startup failures return tool errors; neither
platform silently retries without confinement. Windows skips OS confinement
and retains application policy and approval checks without extra prompts.

The CLI routes shell commands and file tools through the same execution
policy. On Linux/macOS, file tools execute in a fixed-operation sandboxed Python
worker. Approving an external file write grants that target for this call.
Shell `additional_write_paths` must name existing files or directories; a
directory grant includes its descendants. Changing workdir does not expand
write permissions. Approvals never silently grant full host access.

Network access is independent and enabled by default. `--no-network` disables
sandbox network access; approving network access does not grant external file
writes. Windows and `danger-full-access` do not provide OS-level network
restriction. The provider connection runs outside the tool sandbox.

On Linux/macOS, the CLI hides existing user and project `.cade` directories
from sandboxed commands and protects existing Git hooks and Git configuration
from writes. The home directory is not writable by default. Private temp and
common tool caches are redirected to a session directory, cleaned on exit.
Apart from hidden paths, the filesystem remains readable; this is not complete
secret isolation. Restrict credentials and exposed resources accordingly.

MCP server processes and host-managed state run outside the tool sandbox. Treat
their configuration and code as trusted. The sandbox is not a container or VM,
and it does not make an untrusted repository safe.

See [decision 0009](decisions/0009-execution-permissions.md) for the contract.

# Snapshots and goals

<!-- source: snapshots-goals.md -->

# Snapshots and goals

## File snapshots

Cade records a snapshot before a file tool changes a file. Snapshots live
under `.cade/snapshots` with a JSONL index and one directory per snapshot.
Capture appends and syncs one index record. An incomplete final line is ignored
and repaired before the next capture; corrupt complete records block capture.
See [decision 0014](decisions/0014-storage-append-cost.md).

Covered changes:

- `write` and `edit`.
- Simple literal-file shell mutations: `rm`, file-to-file `mv`/`cp`, `touch`,
  `echo` redirection, and `sed -i`. Quoted filenames can contain spaces.
  Directory operands, expansions, and unknown command forms are not captured.
- Creating a file records that it did not exist; undo removes it.

Not covered:

- Complex pipelines, command lists, unknown scripts, and commands that mutate
  files without naming them.
- Files larger than the snapshot limit (5 MiB) are rejected rather than
  silently skipped.
- Directory trees are not copied; directory mutations are skipped.

## Undo

```bash
cade --undo
```

This command uses the same checkpoint recovery as TUI `/undo`. It reverses one
action in the latest session, including its conversation position and tracked
file changes. Use `cade --resume ID --undo` to select a session, then resume that
session in the TUI to `/redo`. It does not contact a provider or start MCP.
See [decision 0013](decisions/0013-unified-cli-undo.md).

Recovery validates all affected files before writing. Conflicts, corrupt
payloads, and unknown outcomes block restoration. Stop external file writers
before any restoration. Standalone file snapshots without owned checkpoints do
not create an undo action.

Snapshots are project state, not session facts. They are not part of the
JSONL session branch.

## Checkpoint recovery

Each root user turn creates a checkpoint before execution. Registered file
mutations retain before/after content, existence, and permissions. Synchronous
subagents share the parent capture scope. Queued inputs get checkpoints when
execution starts; steering remains part of the active turn.

- `/undo` reverses one turn or explicit recovery action; `/redo` reapplies one.
  Neither reruns tools or contacts a provider. History survives restart.
- `/rewind` selects an active-path user prompt, then conversation, code, or both,
  followed by a preview and confirmation. It restores the point before the prompt.
- `/revert` selects a turn range and all or one tracked file. Explicit path
  arguments select multiple files. Conversation stays unchanged.

A new action discards the active redo chain. Old conversation branches remain.
Tree navigation never restores files; a stale undo/redo cannot cross a changed
conversation position. Rewind can still use owned checkpoints and computes code
changes from actual actions, including intervening undo/redo/revert operations.
Copied sessions do not inherit workspace actions. Historical prompts without an
owned checkpoint support conversation-only rewind.

Recovery checks all selected files and content blobs before modifying a file.
A changed target, unknown outcome, corrupt blob, symlink, hard link, or protected
metadata path blocks automatic code restoration. Restoring an older range also
fails if later edits conflict; there is no automatic reverse-patch merge.
File limits apply to both images. A missing post-change image makes that turn's
code checkpoint incomplete rather than pretending that recovery is available.
Unselected files and the user's Git index remain untouched. Directory trees,
untracked shell changes, and external side effects are not restored.

Cooperating operations share `.cade/recovery/workspace.lock`. The action
journal and checkpoint links use closed records under that directory. A
`pending.json` plan stores both images before restoration begins. Files use
atomic per-file replacement; a multi-file restore is not a filesystem-wide
atomic operation. On interruption, resume the named session to finish the plan
idempotently. A third, externally edited state stops recovery without overwriting
that edit. Resolve the reported conflict and resume; do not delete the pending
plan to bypass the write guard. New agent writes remain blocked until it finishes.
External editors do not honor the lock and must be stopped during recovery.
Read-only mode blocks code recovery; conversation-only rewind remains available.
Esc cancels a preview, not a committing file restore. A normal TUI exit waits
for the recovery commit; a forced process interruption uses the pending plan.

Code-only restoration keeps model-visible conversation messages. The next
request receives an audited notice to inspect restored files rather than trust
older tool effects. Settings, credentials, grants, and external services do not
rewind with conversation history.

## Goals

A goal is one durable objective stored in `.cade/goal.json`. It has an
objective, a status (`active` or `done`), and an update time.

```bash
cade --goal "Add a regression test for the parser" "Start the task."
```

In the TUI:

- `/goal` shows the current goal.
- `/goal TEXT` sets an active goal.
- `/goal done` marks it complete.
- `/goal clear` removes it.

The `goal` tool provides the same actions to the model. An active goal is added
to request context so a resumed or compacted session still knows the objective.
Goals are host state; they do not change the session schema.

Goals are intentionally small. Use `NOTE.md` for working details and `MEMORY.md`
for facts that outlive the objective.

# Skills and memory

<!-- source: skills-memory.md -->

# Skills and memory

## Skills

Cade discovers user skills in `~/.cade/skills/` and `~/.agents/skills/`.
Set `trust_project_skills` to `true` to include the matching directories under
this project. Project skills are disabled by default. An explicit `skills_dir`
is trusted and has the highest priority, followed by project and user roots;
`.cade/skills` precedes `.agents/skills` within each scope. Duplicate names
produce a warning and keep the first definition.

Each skill directory must contain `SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: release-check
description: Validate release metadata before tagging.
---

Run the release checklist...
```

The loader validates required fields, naming rules, directory-name agreement,
length limits, and metadata types. Invalid definitions are skipped with a
diagnostic. Discovery reads frontmatter only; activation reads the body and
indexes `references/`, `scripts/`, and `assets/`.

The request carries a compact catalog. The model loads instructions with:

```json
{"name": "release-check"}
```

The result includes the absolute skill root and resource paths. Read a reference
without loading every resource:

```json
{"name": "release-check", "reference": "checklist.md"}
```

Reference names are relative to `references/`; hidden files, symbolic links,
binary references, and paths outside the skill root are rejected. References
are limited to 50 KiB. Scripts run through the ordinary `bash` tool and its
permission policy. Trusted skill directories are readable but protected from
writes in native sandboxes; other private `.cade/` state stays hidden.

Use `$release-check` or `/skill release-check` for explicit activation.
`disable-model-invocation: true` hides a skill from automatic selection while
keeping explicit activation available. `compatibility` is disclosed when loaded;
`allowed-tools` is advisory and never grants permissions.

Bodies are tool-result facts. Previously activated instructions missing after
compaction or a window reset are restored from the active branch into request
context. A model can reload a skill when it needs its exact instructions.

## Memory

`MEMORY.md` at the project root stores durable facts. It is loaded into request
context as `<memory source="MEMORY.md">` on every task, capped at 32 KiB.

The model appends facts with the `memory` tool:

```json
{"text": "Prefer pytest and keep changes minimal."}
```

`memory` writes only `MEMORY.md`; it cannot write arbitrary paths. The file is
capped at 64 KiB for writes. Remove stale entries manually when it fills.

Memory is different from the other state files:

- `AGENTS.md` is project instruction, owned by the project.
- `NOTE.md` is short-lived working state; it is summarized with compaction.
- `MEMORY.md` is a durable preference or convention.
- The session log is the record of what happened.

## Request context

Instructions, skill catalog, `NOTE.md`, `MEMORY.md`, and an active goal are all
request-only context. They appear in each request audit but never become
conversation messages. See [Sessions and context](sessions-context.md).

# MCP

<!-- source: mcp.md -->

# MCP

## Connection and tools

Cade uses the official Python MCP SDK with stdio and Streamable HTTP.
It discovers tools at startup and keeps one connection per server:

```json
{
  "mcp_servers": {
    "files": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["mcp_server.py"],
      "timeout_ms": 30000
    }
  }
}
```

Tools are named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. Their input schema comes from the
server's `tools/list` response. Calls run sequentially over the connection and
preserve server state.

Policy:

- `plan` mode hides MCP tools and denies them.
- `read_only` denies them.
- `build` and `ask` ask by default; a rule can allow a specific tool.

A server that fails to start is reported and skipped. A later request can
reconnect it; calls with unknown outcomes are never automatically repeated.
Cancelling or timing out an active call closes its transport and waits for SDK
cleanup. Connections are also closed when the application session exits.

The default `protocol: "auto"` probes the 2026-07-28 stateless protocol and falls
back to the legacy initialize handshake. `protocol: "legacy"` forces the
handshake. The installed SDK supports the 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18,
2025-11-25, and 2026-07-28 revisions. The negotiated version is recorded with
tool results. Unknown versions are rejected by the SDK.

Tool discovery follows pagination. Legacy list-change notifications refresh the
live tool catalog before the next model request. Stateless connections refresh
the listing at each model request. Ambiguous or overlong host tool names are
excluded with diagnostics. Input arguments and structured outputs are checked
against their JSON Schemas. Progress and result metadata enter the session log.

Servers advertising resources or prompts also expose these permission-gated
operations under the same server prefix: `resources_list`, `resources_read`,
`prompts_list`, and `prompts_get`. List results preserve `nextCursor`; supply it
as `cursor` to read the next page. Returned resources and prompts are untrusted
data, not instructions or authorization.

For HTTP transport and credential configuration, see [Configuration](configuration.md#mcp-servers).

## Limits

MCP extensions, sampling, elicitation, resource subscriptions, and automatic
OAuth login are not enabled. Image, audio, and resource content blocks are
preserved as JSON in Cade's text tool-result contract rather than sent as native
multimodal provider messages. Tool output exceeding the runtime limit is marked
as truncated; exact structured metadata remains in the log.
Schemas must be self-contained: local `$ref` values work, but schema validation
does not fetch external URLs.

# Subagents

<!-- source: subagents.md -->

# Subagents

## Child sessions

The `delegate` tool runs one or more child tasks in separate sessions and
returns their final answers with the child session IDs. Use `prompt` for one task:

```json
{"prompt": "Find the failing test and report the file and line."}
```

The child:

- gets the parent's provider, budget, policy, approver, and request context;
- gets the base tools plus a history tool bound to its own log;
- does not get the `delegate` tool, so it cannot recurse;
- uses at most 20 steps;
- writes its own session under `<sessions>/subagents/`.

The parent records only the tool call and the returned summary. The child log
keeps the detailed evidence.

Use `tasks` for multiple tasks and `mode` to restrict child permissions:

```json
{"tasks": ["Inspect the parser", "Add a regression test"], "mode": "build"}
```

Tasks run sequentially in separate child sessions. Each result includes the
child session ID; the parent gets one combined tool result. Child modes cannot
expand parent permissions: a Plan parent cannot delegate Build work.

## Limits

Subagents are sequential and share the parent's approval context rather than
running in parallel.

# Cookbook

<!-- source: cookbook/README.md -->

# Cookbook

Procedures with a concrete outcome and a verification step. Each recipe names
the mode and the evidence to keep.

- [Fix a bug](fix-a-bug.md): reproduce, patch, verify, report.
- [Add a feature](add-a-feature.md): test, implement, verify, review the diff.
- [Review only](review-only.md): investigate in plan mode without mutations.
- [Run a long session](long-session.md): NOTE, compaction, history, and goals.
- [Connect a custom MCP server](custom-mcp.md): configure, allow, call, inspect.

For command details, see [CLI](../cli.md) and [Configuration](../configuration.md).

# Fix a bug

<!-- source: cookbook/fix-a-bug.md -->

# Fix a bug

Use `build` mode for the change. Keep the patch minimal and verify with the
repository's tests.

## Procedure

1. Reproduce the failure:

   ```bash
   cade --mode plan -p "Read the failing test and explain the failure."
   ```

2. Fix it:

   ```bash
   cade --mode build --yes -p "Fix the failing test with the smallest change, then run pytest."
   ```

3. Inspect the diff and the snapshot:

   ```bash
   git diff
   cade --undo  # only if the change is wrong
   ```

## Verify

- The targeted test passes.
- The full relevant test file passes.
- The diff contains only the intended change.
- The assistant names the command it ran.

## Keep

The run log records the request, tool calls, and test output. The snapshot
allows recovery before the next run. For a reviewable change, keep the diff in
the commit, not in a docs file.

## Avoid

- `--read-only` when you intend to edit.
- `--yes` on a shared repository without rules.
- A broad refactor when a one-line condition fixes the test.

# Add a feature

<!-- source: cookbook/add-a-feature.md -->

# Add a feature

Write the test first, then implement, then verify. Use `build` mode and keep the
diff reviewable.

## Procedure

1. Ask for a failing test or write it yourself:

   ```bash
   cade --mode build --yes -p "Add a test for mul() that asserts 2 * 3 == 6; run it and confirm it fails."
   ```

2. Implement the smallest change:

   ```bash
   cade --mode build --yes -p "Implement mul() and run the new test."
   ```

3. Review:

   ```bash
   git diff
   uv run --locked pytest -q
   ```

## Verify

- The new test fails before the change and passes after it.
- Existing tests still pass.
- The implementation has no unrelated edits.
- Public behavior is documented in the relevant guide.

## Undo

If the change is wrong, use `cade --undo` before starting another attempt.
This reverses one checkpoint action, including conversation position and tracked
file changes. Use `--resume ID --undo` to select a session.

## Keep

Update the guide or decision record when the feature changes a public contract.
Tests belong in `tests/`; docs belong under `docs/`.

# Review only

<!-- source: cookbook/review-only.md -->

# Review only

Use `plan` and `--read-only` when the task is to inspect, not change.

## Procedure

```bash
cade --mode plan --read-only -p "Review the request builder for evidence loss. Cite files and lines; do not modify anything."
```

Plan mode hides write and edit tools and denies mutating shell commands.
`--read-only` also denies memory, MCP, and any remaining mutation.

## Verify

- `git status` is clean.
- The answer cites files by relative path and line.
- Claims about tests name the command and result.
- Findings distinguish a bug from a preference.

## Keep

For a review, keep the report in the conversation or a review document. Do not
create a working note unless the review spans multiple sessions.

## Limits

The model can still read anything inside the workspace. A review of untrusted
code still needs human judgment; the policy prevents writes, not misleading
prose.

# Run a long session

<!-- source: cookbook/long-session.md -->

# Run a long session

Long tasks need durable state and a way to recover context. Use `NOTE.md`, a
goal, and the history tool.

## Procedure

1. Set a goal:

   ```bash
   cade --goal "Migrate the request builder to the new budget model" "Start by mapping the current admission rules."
   ```

2. Keep a working note. Ask the model to update `NOTE.md` after each milestone:

   ```text
   Update NOTE.md with completed work, current blockers, and the next action.
   ```

3. Continue the same session:

   ```bash
   cade --continue "Resume from NOTE.md and run the next step."
   ```

4. Compact when the session grows:

   ```text
   /compact
   ```

5. Recover an old detail:

   ```text
   Use history with query "budget" to find the earlier discussion.
   ```

## Verify

- `NOTE.md` names the next action, not just history.
- A resumed run can continue without the original terminal.
- The goal is marked done only when its acceptance check passes.

## Limits

`NOTE.md` is request context and is summarized during compaction. `MEMORY.md` is
for durable facts, not a task log. The session log is the authority for exact
evidence.

# Connect a custom MCP server

<!-- source: cookbook/custom-mcp.md -->

# Connect a custom MCP server

MCP servers use stdio or Streamable HTTP. Cade keeps one connection per server and exposes each
tool as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`.

## Configure

Add the server to `cade.json`:

```json
{
  "mcp_servers": {
    "files": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["tools/mcp_files.py"],
      "timeout_ms": 30000,
      "env": {"LOG_LEVEL": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

`command` and `args` are required; `cwd`, `env`, and `timeout_ms` are optional.
A relative `cwd` resolves against the project root.

## Allow

MCP tools ask by default. Add a rule for a specific tool if unattended runs need
it:

```json
{
  "rules": [
    {"tool": "mcp__files__read_file", "decision": "allow"}
  ]
}
```

Plan mode and `--read-only` deny MCP tools even with a rule.

## Verify

1. Start Cade; it prints a startup error if the server cannot start.
2. Ask the model to list or call a discovered tool.
3. Check the tool result and the `mcp__` prefix in the log.
4. Stop Cade; the server process closes at exit.

## Limits

See [MCP](../mcp.md) for supported protocol revisions,
resources, prompts, and optional capability limits. An active call that times
out closes its connection and waits for SDK cleanup.

# Hosts

<!-- source: hosts.md -->

# Hosts

Cade has one terminal host with two modes: an interactive TUI and one-shot
execution. Both use the same session log, request builder, tools, policy, and
harness loop. Both modes use `app.bootstrap.create_session` and
`ApplicationSession.run_task`; the TUI also uses the service for commands and
session control.

## Terminal UI

Without `-p` or `exec`, the CLI starts the TUI in an interactive terminal:

```bash
cade
cade "Fix the failing test."
```

A positional task is sent once as the first TUI message. The TUI stays open
after the task completes.

The TUI keeps the conversation in a scrollable transcript, shows streaming
assistant text and tool progress, and handles approvals and questions without
leaving the application. Common keys:

- `Enter` submits a message; while running, it queues, steers, or interrupts according to the busy-input mode.
- `Alt+Enter` steers the running task at the next model step.
- `Alt+S` steers the running task; `Alt+Q` queues a follow-up task. These
  shortcuts submit plain editor text using a fixed action, regardless of the
  busy-input mode selected for `Enter`.
- `Shift+Tab` cycles `ask`, `build`, and `plan`.
- `Esc` interrupts the running task, including a model request that has not
  produced output yet. Undelivered queued input returns to the editor.
- When idle with empty input, double `Esc` opens the `/rewind` checkpoint selector.
  Use `/tree` to navigate branches in the same session, or `/fork` to copy history into a new session.
- `Ctrl+C` clears input without interrupting the task; press it again within
  500 ms to exit.
- `Ctrl+D` twice exits when idle with empty input.
- `Ctrl+O` toggles tool details; `Ctrl+T` toggles reasoning output.
- `Ctrl+Q` exits.

The TUI opens native selectors for models, modes, reasoning effort,
configuration, and permissions. Press `?` or run `/help` for the key and
command reference.

The TUI requires both stdin and stdout to be terminals. In a pipe or a
non-interactive process, use `-p TASK` or `exec TASK`.

The transcript shows context budget failures and output token limits as stopped
turns, including the provider error when available.

## One-shot

With `-p` or `exec`, the CLI runs once and exits:

```bash
cade -p "Fix the failing test."
cade exec "Fix the failing test."
```

One-shot mode supports `--json` for a JSONL event stream. Use `--read-only` or
explicit rules rather than a blanket `--yes` in automation and CI.

# Development

<!-- source: development.md -->

# Development

Cade is maintained independently of Cade. Work from this repository root.

## Setup

You need Python 3.12+ and uv. Linux tool execution also requires usable
bubblewrap (`sudo apt-get install bubblewrap` on Debian/Ubuntu) and a host that
permits unprivileged user namespaces. Denied UID mappings are sandbox startup
errors, not approval failures. CI uses Ubuntu 22.04 without disabling host
security policies. macOS uses system `sandbox-exec`.
File discovery and content search use shell commands. You can install fd and
ripgrep for these operations; they are not required to start Cade:

```bash
# Debian or Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install ripgrep fd-find
# macOS
brew install ripgrep fd
# Windows (Scoop)
scoop install ripgrep fd
```

On Debian/Ubuntu, invoke fd as `fdfind`.

Native sandbox tests run on Linux and macOS; Windows
skips those tests and executes tools directly. General shell regression tests
use PowerShell on Windows and Bash on Linux and macOS. Windows development
requires `pwsh` or `powershell` on PATH; Git Bash is needed only when using the
`bash` tool. CI runs the regression suite on both Linux and Windows.

```bash
uv sync --locked --extra dev --extra docs
mkdir -p tmp test-results
```

Code lives in `src/cade/`, tests in `tests/`, and documentation in `docs/`.
See [Architecture](architecture.md) for module boundaries.

### Restricted uv cache access

If uv cannot open its global cache `.lock` file because access is denied, use
`.uv-cache` inside the workspace. From the repository root in PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:UV_CACHE_DIR = "$PWD\.uv-cache"
```

This setting applies to the current terminal session. Run the usual uv commands
after setting it. For a single command, use
`uv --cache-dir ./.uv-cache run --locked ...` instead. Keep the cache
inside the workspace rather than changing global directory permissions.

## Dependencies

Use `uv add PACKAGE` to add a runtime dependency and `uv add --dev PACKAGE` for
development tools. Let uv generate version requirements and update `uv.lock`;
do not invent version bounds or edit dependency versions by hand. Add an extra
constraint only when a documented compatibility requirement justifies it.
Use `uv remove PACKAGE` to remove a dependency.

## Checks

```bash
uv run --locked ruff check src/cade/ tests/
uv run --locked ruff format --check src/cade/ tests/
uv run --locked pyright src/cade/
uv run --locked pytest -q tests --basetemp=tmp/pytest
uv run --locked cade --help
uv run --locked python -m cade --help
uv run --locked cade login --help
uv run --locked python -m cade.docs check
uv build --no-sources
```

Follow the [validation guidelines](testing.md) to select focused checks.
Use `tmp/` for ordinary temporary workspaces, `test-results/` for regression
reports, and `e2e-results/` for end-to-end test results. Keep caches in dedicated
tool directories. Never commit credentials or raw provider traces.

## Documentation

The docs source is `docs/`. The manifest is `docs/docs.json`; it defines
navigation order and published pages. [docs/README.md](README.md) is the manual
entry point. [docs/AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) defines documentation rules.

```bash
uv run --locked python -m cade.docs catalogs --write
uv run --locked python -m cade.docs llms --write
uv run --locked python -m cade.docs build
uv run --locked python -m cade.docs check
```

`check` validates the manifest, page files, relative links, anchors, and generated
catalogs. It uses only the standard library and runs in CI. `build` renders
`docs/index.html` and needs the `docs` extra.

`llms --write` updates `docs/llms.txt` and `docs/llms-full.txt`. `catalogs --write`
updates the config, event, and module references under `docs/design/`.
Do not edit generated files by hand.

To add a page:

1. Add the Markdown file under `docs/`.
2. Add it to a section in `docs/docs.json`.
3. Use relative links to other pages.
4. Regenerate the catalogs and site, then run the docs check.

Every Markdown file must be listed in the manifest unless it matches `exclude`.
The excluded files are agent instructions, decision records, and the postmortem
template. Put session format references under `docs/reference/` and historical
research under `docs/history/`.

## Boundaries

Cade owns five runtime packages: `ai`, `harness`, `coding`, `app`, and `hosts`.
The harness contains local process execution under `harness/execution/local`.
Lower layers never import higher layers; `tests/test_architecture.py` enforces
these boundaries. Do not add dependencies on the earlier Cade project.

Public interfaces include the session schema, config fields, CLI flags, tool
names, and docs manifest. Change them with tests and documentation in the same
commit.

## Commits and releases

Review the diff and run checks before committing. Do not push or publish without
maintainer approval. Confirm that the Git remote points to this repository, not
the earlier Cade project, before pushing.

The CI workflow checks code, tests, docs, startup, and distribution builds.
Version tags (`vX.Y.Z`) must match `pyproject.toml` and belong to `main`. The
release workflow publishes checked distribution artifacts after approval in the
GitHub `release` environment. Never move a published tag.

# Validation guidelines

<!-- source: testing.md -->

# Validation guidelines

Choose checks for the behavior and risk being changed. Keep ordinary test
workspaces and temporary files under `tmp/`, regression reports under
`test-results/`, and end-to-end test results under `e2e-results/`. Keep tool
caches in their dedicated directories, such as `.uv-cache/` and `.pytest_cache/`.
Do not copy account credentials into test evidence.

## Required checks

After code changes, run:

```bash
mkdir -p tmp test-results
uv run --locked ruff check src/cade/ tests/
uv run --locked ruff format --check src/cade/ tests/
uv run --locked pyright src/cade/
uv run --locked pytest -q tests --basetemp=tmp/pytest
```

After import, package, or entry-point changes, also check:

```bash
uv run --locked cade --help
uv run --locked python -m cade --help
uv run --locked cade login --help
uv build --no-sources
```

For distribution changes, inspect the wheel and install it in a clean virtual
environment. Check startup outside the source tree and confirm that no `cade`
package, command, or dependency is required.

## Execution environment

General shell contracts run through the native shell: PowerShell on Windows,
Bash on Linux and macOS. Use `shell_tool_class` and `python_command` from
`tests/conftest.py` to select the tool and quote Python arguments. Keep the same
behavioral assertions on every platform. Do not substitute PowerShell for a
test that specifically exercises Bash syntax or Bash executable discovery.

Shell cancellation tests must be able to terminate the processes they start.
On Windows, `taskkill /T /F` needs permission to terminate the test's process
tree. If it reports `Access denied`, run the check in an approved execution
environment with that permission.

If uv cannot access its global cache, use the
[workspace cache](development.md#restricted-uv-cache-access). If pytest cannot
write `.pytest_cache`, use `-p no:cacheprovider` to disable its optional cache.
Keep `--basetemp` under `tmp/` in either case.

## Select behavioral checks

- Local computation or policy: use focused regression tests with independently
  checked expectations and edge cases.
- Connected components: test the real components together, controlling only
  external boundaries where needed.
- Provider parsing: use captured, sourced protocol payloads through the adapter.
  Replacing a whole provider tests the application, not the remote protocol.
- Login: test host routing, credential persistence, and failure behavior without
  contacting a live account. Real OAuth acceptance requires explicit approval.
- Real hosts or services: run E2E only when lower-level checks leave a concrete
  workflow risk uncovered. Record the task, prerequisites, commands, expected
  observable results, and independent verification before running it.
- Documentation: check facts, links, commands, generated catalogs, and the diff.

Add reusable tests only for a concrete coverage gap. Tests should protect user
outcomes or explicit contracts, not private implementation details. Do not
change production APIs merely to accommodate tests.

## Report results

State what each check establishes. Separate failures caused by code from missing
permissions, environment prerequisites, or external services. Report checks not
run and remaining risks explicitly. Provider completion text alone is not proof
that a workflow succeeded.

# Cade review standards

<!-- source: review-standards.md -->

# Cade review standards

This document defines how coding agents should review this repository. It is separate from implementation standards: `AGENTS.md` and code standards guide how to write code; this file guides how to judge code.

## Review Goal

Review code for correctness, maintainability, Pythonic design, clean boundaries, and long-term elegance.

Do not treat “tests pass” as sufficient. Passing tests only prove current behavior under current coverage. A review must also judge whether the code is simple, well-shaped, and worth keeping.

Prefer fewer high-quality findings over many minor comments.

## Review Scope

Check for:

* serious bugs and edge-case failures;
* architecture and module-boundary problems;
* security risks and unsafe defaults;
* non-Pythonic or awkward implementation patterns;
* unnecessary abstraction, compatibility layers, indirection, or defensive code;
* duplicated helpers or concepts;
* APIs shaped for tests rather than real usage;
* tests that overfit implementation details;
* code that works but is not clean, separable, or elegant.

## Core Principles

Code should be Pythonic, explicit, typed, and easy to reason about.

Prefer direct design over compatibility scaffolding. Do not preserve backward compatibility unless there is an explicit project requirement.

Tests serve production code. Do not accept awkward production APIs, leaked internals, or distorted boundaries merely because existing tests expect them.

A clean deletion is often better than preserving unused flexibility.

A small amount of duplication is better than premature abstraction. Abstraction is justified only when it clarifies a real shared concept.

Avoid “just in case” design. Flexibility without a concrete caller is usually noise.

## What To Flag

Flag code when it:

* hides simple logic behind unnecessary helpers, classes, registries, factories, or protocols;
* mixes unrelated responsibilities in one module or class;
* creates compatibility paths that are not required by current users;
* uses dynamic imports, untyped escape hatches, broad exception swallowing, or loose dictionaries where typed structures would be clearer;
* makes tests depend on private implementation details instead of observable behavior;
* changes production design only to make tests easier;
* adds comments that explain obvious code instead of clarifying real constraints;
* introduces dependencies, config, or runtime behavior that is broader than the actual need;
* duplicates concepts under different names;
* keeps dead code, unused extension points, or speculative branches.

## What Not To Flag

Do not report pure personal taste.

Do not nitpick formatting that Ruff or the formatter should handle.

Do not request abstraction merely because two pieces of code look similar. First decide whether they express the same concept.

Do not demand backward compatibility unless the repository explicitly requires it.

Do not treat test failures as automatically meaning production code is wrong; the test may be the thing that should change.

## Finding Format

Each finding should include:

* severity: critical, high, medium, or low;
* file path and symbol;
* the problem;
* why it matters;
* the cleanest recommended direction.

Use direct language. If something exists only for compatibility, test convenience, or accidental complexity, say so.

Prefer this format:

```text
[medium] src/cade/example.py::ExampleRunner

Problem:
...

Why it matters:
...

Recommended direction:
...
```

## Severity Guide

Use `critical` for issues that can cause data loss, security exposure, command execution risk, or completely broken core behavior.

Use `high` for likely runtime bugs, incorrect behavior in normal use, unsafe architecture, or design that blocks future work.

Use `medium` for maintainability problems, unclear boundaries, bad abstractions, fragile tests, or non-Pythonic design that will likely create bugs later.

Use `low` for local cleanup opportunities that improve clarity but do not currently distort the design.

Do not inflate severity to make a point.

## Review Output Rules

Do not modify files during review.

Do not produce a long list of minor style comments.

Group related findings when they share the same root cause.

Include file paths and concrete examples.

If the code is mostly good, say so and report only meaningful issues.

If a finding depends on an assumption, state the assumption.

# Parity

<!-- source: parity.md -->

# Parity

Before this project was renamed from Cade Mini to Cade, it was accepted against
the earlier Cade project on two real repository workflows and a session resume.
This page keeps the labels from that run: "Mini" means this project at the time,
and "Cade" means the earlier project. The full report is
[the historical parity acceptance](history/parity-acceptance.md).

## Workflows

Two clean Git repositories started from the same baseline and the same
`AGENTS.md` instruction: "Run pytest after changes. Keep changes minimal."

Bug fix:

- Task: fix `add` in `calc.py` so pytest passes.
- Both agents changed `a - b` to `a + b`, ran pytest, got one passing test, and
  answered `FIXED`.

Feature:

- Task: add `mul(a, b)` and a test.
- Both agents produced the same diff, ran pytest, got two passing tests, and
  answered `PASS`.

Resume:

- Both agents resumed their prior session, recalled `calc.py`, and identified
  the corrected `+` operator.

## Evidence

- Mini ran with `--mode build --yes`; Cade ran with `--mode build --approval
  auto-review`.
- Both used DeepSeek `deepseek-chat` at the time of the run. Cade now
  supports only the Responses protocol.
- Mini used five steps per workflow; Cade used four. Mini issued an extra `glob`
  inspection, which did not change the result.
- Cade emits JSONL telemetry and budget/approval events; Mini emits human tool
  progress and appends request/run facts to its session log.

## Differences

- Mini's snapshots cover write/edit and common single-command shell mutations;
  complex pipelines are not covered.
- Mini's MCP client is persistent per server but has a narrower capability
  surface than Cade's.
- The OS sandbox is not implemented; Mini relies on path boundaries, modes,
  shell classification, and approvals.
- The earlier live Codex acceptance passed: write created `codex.txt`, and a
  resumed Codex session read it back.

The parity report records the concrete fixtures and observed results. Re-run a
workflow by creating a clean fixture, running both agents with the same provider
and settings, and comparing the diff and test result rather than the prose
answer. Cade supports only the Responses protocol.

# Postmortems

<!-- source: postmortem/README.md -->

# Postmortems

A postmortem records an incident that escaped the intended design. It is the
only place for chronology and war stories; current behavior belongs in the
subsystem reference.

## Records

- [0001: Compaction cut pointed at a shadowed user entry](0001-compaction-cut-misalignment.md)
- [0002: One huge tool result exhausted the request budget](0002-single-huge-tool-result.md)

## Template

Copy [TEMPLATE.md](TEMPLATE.md). Keep the timeline factual, name the root cause,
show the fix, and record the test that would have caught it. Do not turn the
postmortem into a tutorial; link the current behavior page instead.

Postmortems are excluded from the published guide manifest but remain valid
links and are reviewed with the fix.

# 0001: Compaction cut pointed at a shadowed user entry

<!-- source: postmortem/0001-compaction-cut-misalignment.md -->

# 0001: Compaction cut pointed at a shadowed user entry

Date: 2026-10-18

Status: resolved

## Impact

After a prior compaction, the next compaction could choose a `first_kept_id`
from a user entry that was already shadowed. The summary covered the wrong tail,
and the retained window could omit the current task.

## Timeline

- The compactor collected all user entries from the branch.
- It collected user positions from the visible projection.
- It chose a cut by visible position but indexed the full branch entry list.
- A session with a prior compaction therefore pointed at an older, shadowed
  user entry.

## Root cause

Two lists with different lengths were treated as parallel arrays. A compaction
removes old user entries from the projection but leaves them in the branch. The
index into visible positions is not an index into all branch users.

## Fix

The compactor now aligns with the **last N** user entries, where N is the number
of visible user messages. A regression test builds a session with a prior
summary, a retained turn, and a new task, then asserts the new cut points at the
new task and the summary request contains the prior summary.

## Verification

`test_compaction.py::test_iterative_compaction_includes_prior_summary`
passes. The projected roles are `system, summary, user`.

## Follow-up

Any future cut logic must derive entry IDs from the same visible sequence it uses
to choose positions. See [Context and compaction](../subsystems/context-compaction.md).

# 0002: One huge tool result exhausted the request budget

<!-- source: postmortem/0002-single-huge-tool-result.md -->

# 0002: One huge tool result exhausted the request budget

Date: 2026-10-18

Status: resolved

## Impact

A single tool result larger than the input budget could make a request
impossible. The request builder protected the most recent four tool results, so
a lone huge result was never replaced, and the run ended with `context_error`.

## Timeline

- A tool returned a result larger than the budget.
- Admission protected the result because it was among the latest four.
- Turn dropping removed old turns but not the current turn's huge result.
- The request remained over budget and the run failed.

## Root cause

The pruning policy treated "recent" as always protected. Protection is a
heuristic for preserving working evidence, not a hard invariant. With only one
result, the protected set was the entire candidate set.

## Fix

Admission now prunes in passes:

1. Replace unprotected results, oldest first.
2. If still over, replace protected results oldest first.
3. If still over, replace the newest result as a last resort.

Every replacement points to the history tool, so the evidence remains
retrievable. A regression test covers a single huge result.

## Verification

`test_request.py::test_build_prunes_a_single_huge_tool_result` passes and
the resulting request is under budget.

## Follow-up

Keep the history tool available whenever pruning can remove the newest result.
See [Projection and request](../subsystems/projection-request.md).

# Persistence

<!-- source: persistence/README.md -->

# Persistence

Cade stores conversation history in a session log. Other stores have
separate responsibilities.

## Current structure

- Session logs use one closed schema without a format-version field. See
  [Session log schema](../reference/session-schema.md).
- Each entry is one JSON object followed by a newline.
- Sessions live under `.cade/sessions`.
- Compaction, windows, navigation, and recovery are entries, not history rewrites.
- File images live under `.cade/snapshots`; recovery actions and pending
  transactions live under `.cade/recovery`.
- Goals, NOTE, memory, and config remain separate artifacts.

Development changes can break persisted structures. Readers and writers support
only the current structure. There are no compatibility readers or migrations.
See [Change policy](change-policy.md).

## Verification

`test_log.py`, `test_session_history.py`, `test_projection.py`, and
`test_recovery.py` verify validation, projection, copies, and interrupted
recovery. Invalid input must fail before changing durable state.

See the [Persistence catalog](../design/persistence-catalog.md) for ownership and
locations.

# Change policy

<!-- source: persistence/change-policy.md -->

# Change policy

Cade is under active development. Persisted data has one current, closed
structure with no format-version fields. Breaking changes are allowed. Do not
add compatibility readers, migration commands, or special handling for earlier
formats.

## Rules

- Update producers, readers, tests, and field-level documentation together.
- Validate records before modifying durable state.
- Keep conversation history append-only during normal operation.
- Never infer missing request contents from current provider behavior.
- Keep audit facts out of conversation projection.
- Document each new field's owner and lifetime.
- Use a decision record for changes to durable behavior or ownership.

Verify current behavior and failure recovery with focused tests. Generated
catalogs and documentation must match the implementation. See
[Session log schema](../reference/session-schema.md) and
[Persistence](README.md).

# Upgrade guide

<!-- source: upgrade/README.md -->

# Upgrade guide

Cade is under active development. Breaking changes are allowed. Persisted
records have one current structure, with no compatibility or migration layer.
See [Change policy](../persistence/change-policy.md).

## Rename from Cade Mini

The distribution, Python package, command, configuration file, and state
directories are now `cade`. The tool does not read the old paths. To keep
existing data, move it before the first run:

```bash
mv ~/.cade-mini ~/.cade
mv .cade-mini .cade
mv cade-mini.json cade.json
```

Repeat the project moves in each workspace that used the old name. Sessions,
snapshots, goals, skills, and credentials keep working after the move.

## Sign in with ChatGPT

Use `chatgpt` for ChatGPT plan usage and `cade login` for Sign in with
ChatGPT. For API-key authentication, use `openai` or `deepseek`. Credentials live
under `~/.cade/`. See [CLI authentication](../cli.md#login).

## Session and workspace recovery

`/tree` preserves conversation branches. `/undo` and `/redo` reverse or reapply
one action. `/rewind` selects a checkpoint and restoration scope; idle double
Esc opens its selector. `/revert` restores selected tracked file changes without
trimming conversation.

Checkpoint ownership and action history belong to their original session.
Copied conversations do not inherit a workspace undo stack. CLI `--undo` now
uses the same checkpoint recovery as TUI `/undo`; its former file-only behavior
is removed. Standalone snapshots without owned checkpoints are not undo actions. See
[Sessions and context](../sessions-context.md) and
[Recovery coverage](../snapshots-goals.md#checkpoint-recovery).

## Explicit context reduction

The loop tries compaction, then a logged window fallback. If the request remains
over budget, it returns `context_error`. It does not silently trim request-only
history. See [Sessions and context](../sessions-context.md#request-admission).

## Development changes

Update callers, tests, and documentation with each breaking change. Do not
invent missing historical data or rewrite sessions during normal operation.
Pending workspace recovery must complete before new agent writes are allowed;
see the recovery guide for interruption handling.

# Cade Mini: a full refactor of Cade's core

<!-- source: history/design-proposal.md -->

# Cade Mini: a full refactor of Cade's core

> Historical record from before the standalone project split. Package names,
> paths, and development plans below describe that earlier checkout. For the
> current project, see the [manual](../README.md) and
> [architecture](../architecture.md).

> Status: proposal, revised after review. This is a plan, not a reduced feature
> list. Cade Mini is the same product idea with a corrected structure.

## Summary

Cade Mini reimplements Cade on one pipeline: a session log records facts, a
deterministic projection derives model-visible history, a request builder turns
that history plus current inputs into one request, and a loop executes tools.
Everything else attaches to that pipeline through explicit seams.

Mini is not a smaller Cade. It is a full replacement that keeps Cade's
capabilities, removes redundant layers, and adds features only when the pipeline
can carry them. The first increment is the smallest version that proves the
pipeline end to end on the maintainer's daily provider. It is not the final
feature set.

Three corrections from the first draft:

- There is no line budget. The requirement is simple, direct, efficient, and
  elegant code. A structural review decides whether a change belongs, not a line
  count.
- The first increment supports the maintainer's Codex account. A Codex path is
  not a later phase.
- Compaction and window switching are part of the first increment. They are
  projection semantics, not optional features. Compaction is the default;
  window switching is explicit and is the fallback when compaction cannot help.

## Implementation status

Committed on `experiment/cade-mini`:

- Done: session schema, types, append-only log, deterministic projection, pure
  request admission, agent loop, Codex provider and credential store, six
  workspace tools with a policy, compaction and window reset, CLI/REPL with
  resume, project instructions, session listing/titles/`--continue`, project
  configuration, session approval, history retrieval, tool-result pruning,
  iterative compaction, automatic window fallback, skills, composable prompt
  modules, NOTE working state, plan/build/act modes, static rules, session
  grants, shell command classification (no OS sandbox), fork/clone/tree/rewind
  and undo-N, independent subagents and delegate, @/!/$ REPL input, concurrent
  REPL steering/queue with routed approvals, durable project memory, tool
  lifecycle hooks, a persistent stdio MCP bridge, file snapshots/undo covering
  common shell mutation targets, workspace goals, automatic approval review, a
  local web host, a documentation system with design, subsystem, cookbook,
  postmortem, persistence, and upgrade pages, generated
  config/event/module/tool catalogs, a link/anchor checker, generated site,
  `llms.txt`, and `llms-full.txt`, and 219 tests.
- A real CLI acceptance run through the configured DeepSeek account passed: the
  model used the write and read tools, `hello.txt` contained `mini`, and a
  resumed run on the same session read the file and answered `mini`.
- A second real run used `cade-mini.json` and `AGENTS.md`; the model followed the
  project instruction and answered `ZEBRA`. `--list-sessions` showed the session
  title derived from the first user input.
- A real compaction run passed: the first turn produced 21k characters, the
  second turn triggered compaction, and the resulting projection was
  `system, summary, user, assistant` with a completed answer.
- A real skills run passed: the model called the `skill` tool, loaded the
  `orange` skill, and answered `ORANGE`; NOTE.md and AGENTS.md were in context.
- A real build-mode run passed: without `--yes`, the model used the write tool
  and created `build.txt` with content `build-mode`.
- A real web-host run passed: an HTTP POST to `/api/task` returned
  `{"answer":"WEB-OK","termination":"completed"}` from DeepSeek.
- The Mini docs are built from `docs/` and `docs.json`. `python -m
  cade.mini.docs check` validates links and anchors in CI; `build` writes
  `docs/index.html`; `llms --write` writes the catalog and full corpus.
- Parity acceptance passed on two repository workflows and a session resume:
  Mini and Cade produced the same bug-fix and feature diffs, both ran pytest,
  and both recalled the earlier fix. See [Parity acceptance](parity-acceptance.md).
- A persistent MCP subprocess test discovers `echo` and `counter` tools, calls
  them across event loops, and gets `echo:hi` plus stateful `count:1`/`count:2`.
- A live Codex acceptance passed after the quota recovered: the write tool
  created `codex.txt` with `codex-ok`, and a resumed Codex session used the read
  tool and returned `codex-ok`; both runs completed. Earlier attempts during
  quota exhaustion returned HTTP 429 and were recorded as `provider_error`.
- Cade Mini has no OS sandbox; path boundaries, mode policy, shell
  classification, and approvals remain the active safety layer.
- Snapshots cover write/edit and common single-command shell mutations; complex
  pipelines are not snapshotted.
- Milestone acceptance is complete; the remaining items are the platform and
  capability limits listed above, not blockers.

## 1. What Cade is today

Product Python is about 41,000 lines, plus about 5,000 lines of tests. The
repository has 1,387 commits since 2026-05-29.

| Area | Approx. lines | What it owns |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Hosts: TUI, exec, web | 7,900 | prompt_toolkit UI, streaming presentation, HTTP/WebSocket server |
| Agent runtime | 4,700 | runs, inbox, composition generations, tool gate, goal, subagents |
| Agent core | 4,600 | loop, request assembly, context policy, tool scheduling |
| Security and sandbox | 4,200 | permission model, rule DSL, approvals, grants, shell analysis, bubblewrap |
| Coding tools | 3,400 | read, write, edit, glob, grep, bash, web, question, subagent |
| Session and undo | 3,200 | JSONL tree, replay, surface, artifacts, history retrieval, snapshots |
| Providers and auth | 4,000 | seven transports, streaming, usage, OAuth, model registry |
| Product services, config, CLI | 5,900 | assembly, commands, completion, settings, config wizard, entry point |
| Extensions | 3,500 | MCP, skills, memory, hooks, observability |

User-visible capabilities:

- Session continuity: project sessions, resume, fork, clone, tree, rewind, undo,
  snapshots.
- Context: dynamic sections, NOTE handoff, token budgets, evidence previews,
  artifacts, automatic rollover, history search and exact read.
- Execution: plan/build/act modes, rule DSL, approval routers, session and
  permanent grants, LLM approval reviewer, Linux bubblewrap sandbox.
- Models: OpenAI Chat/Responses/Codex, DeepSeek, GLM, MiMo, custom; main,
  subagent, reviewer, judge, and refiner profiles.
- Tools: read, write, edit, glob, find, ls, grep, bash, webfetch, websearch,
  question, history, memory, skills, MCP, subagents.
- Hosts: terminal UI, noninteractive exec, browser workspace.
- Operations: audit JSONL, correlation IDs, provider request records, external
  hooks.

The pipeline itself is about 7,000 lines. The other 34,000 lines are product
surface, safety policy, hosts, and workarounds for the back-edges described in
section 4.

## 2. The core idea and the primary invariant

One sentence: **Cade keeps a durable, inspectable record of what happened, and
gives the model a deterministic view of that record, while effects happen only
through typed tools.**

The working rule is the one Dsh states as **model-visible means logged**: every
model-visible message must be reconstructable from the session log. A new
model-visible input needs a logged fact. A log-only record is allowed, but it
never projects into model history.

Four invariants:

1. **Facts are durable and append-only.** User input, model output, tool results,
   and compaction decisions are recorded before they are relied on. Recovery is
   re-derivation, not reconstruction from process memory.
2. **History is a projection.** `project(log_branch) -> conversation` is pure,
   deterministic, and independent of process state. It contains no stored
   projection and no mutable working copy.
3. **A request is a snapshot.** `build(conversation, context, tools, budget) ->
   request` is pure. It may drop content to fit the budget and reports what it
   dropped. It never writes history.
4. **Effects go through tools under policy.** The loop decides what to call; the
   policy decides whether it may start; the workspace is the effect surface.

The differentiating part is invariants 1 and 2. A streaming loop, tool parsing,
and file tools are table stakes. The lossless transcript behind a lossy window,
the branchable session, and the auditable request are Cade's identity.

### Three planes, one log

The log contains three kinds of records. Only the first is projected:

| Plane | Examples | Projected? | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Conversation | `user`, `assistant`, `tool_result`, `system`, `compaction` | Yes | Model-visible history |
| Request | `request` | No | Exact request envelope, dynamic context, token estimate, dropped ids |
| Operational | `run`, `attempt`, `window`, `meta` | No | Lifecycle, failures, hard boundaries, metadata |

`window` is a decision that changes where projection starts. It is log-only
because it produces no message of its own; an optional handoff summary is a
separate conversation fact.

The latest `system` event is always projected first and is never shadowed by
compaction. Log a new one when the base prompt changes. Dynamic context such as
the environment, `AGENTS.md`, and the current mode is request-only.

This separation satisfies "model-visible means logged" without pretending that
the current environment, `AGENTS.md`, or a failed attempt is conversation.

### Record shapes

One JSON object per line. A branch is a parent chain; the head is the last entry.

```json
{"v":1,"id":"e1","parent":null,"ts":"...","type":"meta","data":{"session":"s1","project":"C:/repo"}}
{"v":1,"id":"e2","parent":"e1","ts":"...","type":"user","data":{"text":"Fix the test","source":"user"}}
{"v":1,"id":"e3","parent":"e2","ts":"...","type":"assistant","data":{"blocks":[{"type":"text","text":"..."},{"type":"tool_call","id":"c1","name":"bash","args":{"command":"pytest -q"}}],"model":"...","provider":"...","usage":{"input":1200,"output":80},"provider_state":null}}
{"v":1,"id":"e4","parent":"e3","ts":"...","type":"tool_result","data":{"call_id":"c1","status":"ok","content":"3 passed"}}
```

A `system` event carries `{text}`; the latest one is projected first. A `summary`
message is emitted from a `compaction` event, not stored as a message.

## 3. The one-way pipeline

```text
Session log (conversation + request + operational facts)
      │  project()            pure; reads conversation facts and window decisions
      ▼
Conversation (immutable)
      │  build()              pure; adds request-only context; admits to budget
      ▼
Request (ephemeral) ────────► provider
      │
      ▼
Tool calls ──► effects ──► tool results ──► append to log
```

Definitions:

- `Log` is an ordered set of typed facts on a branch.
- `Project(log) -> Conversation` is pure and deterministic. It rejects a
  malformed branch with a specific error.
- `Build(conversation, context, tools, budget) -> Request` is pure. It reports
  what it dropped; it does not write.
- `Run(log, input) -> events + new facts` is the only writer.

Rules:

- **R1. One fact, one record.** A tool call appears in the assistant fact, not
  twice. The final answer is the last assistant text, not a separate fact.
- **R2. No derived content in the log.** A stored message list, a rendered
  preview used as history, or a display summary is not a fact. Large tool output
  may live in an immutable blob; the log stores a stable reference, and the
  projection resolves it.
- **R3. Decisions are facts; projections are not.** A compaction boundary or a
  window start may be logged. The messages they produce are recomputed.
- **R4. Request context is logged but not projected.** The base system prompt is
  a `system` conversation fact when it changes. Dynamic context, the model
  route, tool schemas, token estimates, and dropped ids are request facts.
- **R5. Failures are log-only.** A failed attempt is an `attempt` fact. It does
  not become a fake assistant message.
- **R6. Budget admission belongs to the request.** Compaction belongs to the
  loop, because it appends a fact. A request builder never calls a model.

## 4. Current leaks

These are the back-edges that make the current code hard to maintain.

1. **The projection is written into the log.** A rollover stores the complete
   encoded replacement surface in `context_window_reset`
   ([recorder.py](https://github.com/reddishJade/cade/blob/main/src/cade/harness/session/recorder.py) `record_context_window_reset`,
   [surface.py](https://github.com/reddishJade/cade/blob/main/src/cade/harness/session/surface.py) applies `replacement` at
   replay). Replay then depends on output produced by an older version of the
   projection code, not only on facts.
2. **Request assembly mutates history.** `DefaultRequestAssembler.assemble`
   rewrites `context.messages` in place
   ([request.py](https://github.com/reddishJade/cade/blob/main/src/cade/agent/request.py)). `call_provider` appends a
   `ContextMessage` to history while sending the request
   ([_provider.py](https://github.com/reddishJade/cade/blob/main/src/cade/agent/_provider.py)). Request construction is
   therefore also a state update.
3. **One fact is recorded several times.** The final answer is stored again in
   the `final` event and in an `assistant` record, on top of the assistant
   event's text; replay de-duplicates it with a heuristic
   ([recorder.py](https://github.com/reddishJade/cade/blob/main/src/cade/harness/session/recorder.py),
